title: What am I missing with Fanny and Alexander?

commenti.body: I haven't seen it for quite a few years so I don't have anything very interesting to say about it. Only that I felt the same way when I watched it. I thought it was one of his less interesting films. As for why it's so esteemed, it's one of his most conventional films, so it appeals to a larger number of people. And it's long. Nowadays at least, in internet circles, being incredibly long gets a prestige film high praises.

Persona is hands down his best film. To me, that's what "Bergman" is. Through A Glass Darkly, Hour of the Wolf, and The Seventh Seal are also good. But yeah, there are movies like this and Autumn Sonata that just seem boring as hell and I have no idea why people regard them as great.

(Apologies in advance - these are some disorganised, spontaneous reactions to your post. They aren't organised into a succinct comment. But Fanny And Alexander is so massive it's difficult to respond in a succinct manner.) 

The original version of Fanny And Alexander was made for television. It's not meant to be watched all in one go. It's a TV series in five (I think?) episodes. 

Characters like Uncle Carl make more sense when you view the piece in episodes. My interpretation: The first episode (where Uncle Carl gets his big scenes) is very much an exercise in world building. We're establishing Alexander's universe, and all the characters in it. It's warm, comfortable, full of love. But it also contains darkness, death, and, perhaps most importantly, confusion. Carl and Gustav Adolf are brothers, close in age. But look at the great difference between them. Look at the life force that is Gustav Adolf - his capacity for joy. Then look at Carl, steeped in misery and bitterness. How does this happen? It's very real - it's very true to life. These are the mysteries of real life. Alexander's world contains darkness, contradictions and mystery - but it makes sense. It's contained. It's *comprehensible*. This is what the narrative will return to at the end with Gustav Adolf's beautiful speech at the Christening. *Life my be comprehensible*. And human beings must make it so, because unless we make it so, it isn't, and that is awful. Alexander and his family don't appreciate this until they leave their little world and return again. This is what episode one does - it establishes what they are about to leave and what they return to. 

Another note on the first episode - on repeated viewing you see how much of the narrative is foreshadowed during the family Christmas. When you begin to appreciate that it's so impressive - you realise Bergman is a master story teller. 

Another note on Carl - later in the drama we see a kind of repeat of Carl's fight with his wife (when they're arriving home from the boat trip at the summer house). But this time the scene is comic. Viewed by Helena from a distance, Carl and his wife make a ridiculous pair. Tragedy is funny - comedy is sad - nothing is fixed in Fanny And Alexander. It is, in part, a drama about the impermanence of things - the absence of solid ground. We have to make the ground *seem* solid.

Hamlet came into conflict with his Stepfather after his Father died. This is what happens to Alexander also. 

Alexander sees ghosts. During the first 60 seconds of the piece he sees death dragging its scythe. Both he and Fanny see the ghost of their father (leading us to believe that ghosts really do exist in their world). But Alexander is also blessed/cursed with a deep and lively imagination. How much of what he sees is real and how much imagined we don't know. But considering this is a piece about how much of our reality we create with our imagination, that is as it should be. 

Alexander is not the only character to see ghosts (Fanny and Helena also see them), and we also see explicit examples of magic (Uncle Isak's rescue of the children and Alexander's magical participation in the death of his Stepfather). This is universe where God does not exist (he's revealed as a puppet). Fanny And Alexander establishes a non-Christian morality. Good and evil are merged, and what is 'right' is far from obvious. Alexander, it could be argued, murders his Stepfather. How are we to view him after this event? How does Bergman encourage us to view him? I don't get the feeling he wants us to damn Alexander - I get the feeling he wants us to be on Alexander's side. What morality is this? 

God doesn't exist, but magic absolutely does. Great mystery exists in the world, and this is both wonderful and terrifying. I get the feeling this is something Bergman truly believed at this stage in his life.

I think as a film appreciator at some point you have to just let go and say "some things other people like just really aren't for me." We think we can be purely objective with enough films under our belt but we can't.

I know cause I've been struggling with this a lot lately. Like, right now, I really want to write a post asking "What did I miss in Godzilla Minus One" cause lots of other people seem to love it and I thought it was predictable, average in the worst way. Okay, yeah, decent characterization but has this not been the bare minimum expected from a story?

In any case instead of ranting about that elsewhere I'd write this to you personally. And no, can't answer your question about Fanny and Alexander ... haven't seen it - probably wont. But my favorite Bergman has been Wild Strawberries (The Seventh Seal bored me to sleep). 

So if you're looking to appreciate Bergman and you're perhaps a little like me I think Wild Strawberries has the least appreciated of Bergman's sweetness.
